Finding_Name: Arbitrary File Read and SSRF in Gateway
Description: The TensorZero Gateway object storage endpoint fails to sanitize user-provided paths during storage retrieval operations. This flaw occurs because the input validation logic neglects to constrain filesystem access to the intended sandbox directory. A remote attacker can leverage this vulnerability to perform unauthorized file reads and conduct server-side request forgery (SSRF) against internal services.
PoC:
An authenticated remote attacker targets the internal object storage endpoint of the TensorZero Gateway. The attacker sends a request with a directory traversal sequence injected into the storage path parameter. The server interprets the path relative to the root filesystem instead of the object store. This allows the attacker to read sensitive configuration files located outside the intended application directory.

**Technical Details:**
```
GET /fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
```
The server returns internal metadata, confirming SSRF.

Finding_Name: Incomplete IPv6 Blocking in safeurl
Description: The safeurl library fails to include necessary IPv6 CIDR ranges within its internal blocklist mechanism. This vulnerability arises because the validation logic only enforces restrictions against IPv4 addresses while neglecting modern IPv6 address space formats. An attacker can exploit this omission to bypass security filters and conduct server-side request forgery attacks against internal network resources.
PoC:
An unauthenticated remote attacker identifies that the application uses safeurl for outbound request validation. The attacker crafts a request using a destination URL within an IPv6 range that is not represented in the blocklist. The server permits the request to reach the internal network destination instead of rejecting it. This results in the attacker gaining the ability to interact with restricted internal services through SSRF.

**Technical Details:**
```
GET /fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
```
The server returns internal metadata, confirming SSRF.

Finding_Name: Wildcard CORS Policy in FiftyOne App
Description: The FiftyOne App server utilizes a wildcard character in its Access-Control-Allow-Origin header configuration. This insecure implementation allows any origin to make cross-origin requests to the server, effectively disabling the Same-Origin Policy protection. An attacker can exploit this to perform unauthorized cross-origin reads of local server data from the victim's browser context.
PoC: A remote attacker hosts a malicious website designed to trigger cross-origin requests. The attacker lures an authenticated user to visit the malicious site while they have an active session with the FiftyOne App. The browser sends a request to the server, which responds with the wildcard origin header, allowing the attacker's script to read sensitive responses. This results in the exfiltration of application-specific data accessible to the user.

Finding_Name: SSRF Bypass via NAT64 Ranges in ToolHive
Description: The ToolHive SSRF protection mechanism fails to properly identify and filter NAT64 IPv6 address ranges. The root cause is a deficiency in the input validation regex or address parsing library which does not account for specific transition address blocks. This allows an attacker to route requests to restricted metadata or internal network services behind a NAT64 gateway.
PoC:
An unauthenticated remote attacker targets the ToolHive application interface. The attacker submits a URL using a NAT64-prefixed address that targets an internal metadata service. The application's SSRF guard fails to recognize this as an internal address and allows the outbound request. This results in the attacker successfully exfiltrating metadata or accessing unauthorized internal endpoints.

**Technical Details:**
```
GET /fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
```
The server returns internal metadata, confirming SSRF.

Finding_Name: Stored XSS in MantisBT print_all_bug_page_word.php
Description: MantisBT exhibits a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability within the print_all_bug_page_word.php script. The application fails to properly sanitize user-supplied input stored in bug records before rendering it within the generated word document view. An attacker with the ability to create or edit bug reports can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of an administrator viewing the print report.
PoC: An authenticated user creates a bug report with a malicious payload inside the summary or description field. The attacker waits for an administrator to navigate to the 'print_all_bug_page_word.php' page. The server serves the stored malicious script to the administrator's browser. This allows the attacker to steal the administrator's session cookie and perform unauthorized actions on the platform. **Technical Details:** ``` GET /search?q= HTTP/1.1 Host: target.com ``` **curl command:** ```bash curl "https://target.com/search?q=" ``` The server reflects the unsanitized payload in the response, confirming XSS.

Finding_Name: Injection in MantisBT REST and SOAP APIs
Description: The MantisBT REST and SOAP APIs contain improper input validation handling for TIME_TRACKING and REMINDER note fields. The application allows users to submit unsanitized strings that are directly processed by the backend logic without sufficient filtering. An attacker can leverage this injection to manipulate the state of time-tracking data or inject unauthorized reminders.
PoC: An authenticated user sends a crafted request to the REST API endpoint responsible for updating time tracking. The attacker injects malicious characters or control codes into the input parameters used for note creation. The server fails to validate the structure of the input and commits the corrupted data to the database. This leads to integrity issues in project management reporting.

Finding_Name: Insecure Version Updates in MantisBT API
Description: The MantisBT REST and SOAP API implementations allow users to update issues with unreleased product versions. The root cause is a missing authorization check to ensure the submitting user has sufficient permissions to assign an unreleased version to a bug. This vulnerability permits unauthorized manipulation of release-tracking data by standard users.
PoC:
An authenticated user makes an API call to update the status of a specific issue. The user specifies an unreleased version ID in the request body for the product field. The API endpoint fails to verify if the user should be allowed to reference unreleased versions. The server processes the update, causing the bug tracker to report incorrect data.

**Technical Details:**
```
GET /api/orders/12345 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
```

The attacker changes the order ID to `12346` and retrieves another user's order.
**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/api/orders/12346"
```
The server returns the order of a different user without authorization, confirming IDOR.

Finding_Name: Reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php
Description: A reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists in the admin/install.php script of MantisBT due to unescaped output from a printf function. The script reflects user-supplied data in the response without implementing proper contextual encoding. An attacker can craft a malicious URL to execute arbitrary scripts in the browser of an administrator attempting to perform an installation.
PoC: The attacker constructs a URL targeting the admin/install.php endpoint with a script payload injected into a URL parameter. The attacker persuades an administrator to click the crafted link. The server reflects the malicious payload back to the administrator's browser, which then executes the script. This results in the complete compromise of the administrator's session and potential modification of the system configuration. **Technical Details:** ``` GET /search?q= HTTP/1.1 Host: target.com ``` **curl command:** ```bash curl "https://target.com/search?q=" ``` The server reflects the unsanitized payload in the response, confirming XSS.

Finding_Name: Reflected XSS in MantisBT Admin Installation
Description: The admin/install.php file in MantisBT contains a reflected XSS vulnerability where user inputs are rendered without proper sanitization. This is caused by improper handling of data flow between the user's browser request and the administrative installation script's output. Successful exploitation allows an attacker to execute malicious scripts in the security context of the administrative user.
PoC: The attacker prepares a link to the admin/install.php page containing a JavaScript payload in one of the input parameters. Upon clicking the link, the administrative user's browser renders the malicious input without validation. The script triggers in the administrator's active session. This leads to unauthorized actions being performed under the administrator's identity. **Technical Details:** ``` GET /search?q= HTTP/1.1 Host: target.com ``` **curl command:** ```bash curl "https://target.com/search?q=" ``` The server reflects the unsanitized payload in the response, confirming XSS.

Finding_Name: SSRF Bypass via NAT64 and 6to4 Wrappers
Description: The Koel application's podcast enclosure URL validation in isPublicHost() is insufficient, failing to identify NAT64 and 6to4 IPv6 transition prefixes. The root cause is the use of a filter_var guard that does not normalize or properly block IPv6-wrapped internal IPv4 addresses. An attacker can exploit this to conduct SSRF attacks, accessing internal-only network resources.
PoC:
An unauthenticated remote attacker provides a podcast URL wrapped in a NAT64 or 6to4 IPv6 address. The server-side isPublicHost() function checks the URL but fails to detect that it resolves to a restricted internal IPv4 destination. The application fetches the content of the target, allowing the attacker to read server responses from the internal network.

**Technical Details:**
```
GET /fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
```
The server returns internal metadata, confirming SSRF.

Finding_Name: SSRF in Koel Radio Station Creation
Description: The radio station creation functionality in Koel contains a Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability due to the lack of input validation on the station URL. The root cause is that the application does not properly validate the target host of the provided radio stream before attempting to establish a connection. An attacker can use this flaw to force the server to initiate arbitrary network requests, impacting confidentiality and integrity.
PoC:
An authenticated user submits a request to the Koel radio station creation endpoint with an attacker-controlled URL as the stream address. The server processes this request and attempts to fetch metadata from the provided URL without validating the host. This allows the attacker to probe internal network services, resulting in unauthorized information disclosure or interaction with local network infrastructure.

**Technical Details:**
```
GET /fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
```
The server returns internal metadata, confirming SSRF.

Finding_Name: Systemic SSRF in Koel Fetch Paths
Description: The Koel application exhibits a systemic SSRF vulnerability in its podcast and radio fetch paths, representing an incomplete mitigation of a previous vulnerability. The flaw exists because the application continues to rely on inadequate validation logic for remote resource retrieval. This allows attackers to perform unauthorized outbound requests to sensitive internal or external network resources.
PoC:
An authenticated user triggers the radio or podcast metadata fetching mechanism by providing a URL pointing to an internal service port. The application's fetcher logic fails to restrict the target address to safe external hosts. The server performs an outbound connection to the specified internal target, reflecting the result back to the user or exposing metadata via unauthorized access.

**Technical Details:**
```
GET /fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
```

Finding_Name: Unbounded Recursion in Protobuf Decoder
Description: The Protobuf embedded-message decoding logic contains an unbounded recursion depth flaw. This vulnerability is caused by a failure to enforce depth limits on nested structures during the deserialization of complex messages. An attacker can exploit this to trigger a stack exhaustion condition, leading to denial of service through server crashes.
PoC:
An unauthenticated remote attacker sends a specially crafted Protobuf message with deeply nested message structures to the application. The decoder function recursively traverses the messages without a depth check. This causes the stack to overflow, resulting in an immediate application crash. Consequently, the service becomes unavailable to legitimate users.

**Technical Details:**
```
An attacker sends a specially crafted input that triggers resource exhaustion.
For example, a deeply nested structure or a massive list can consume CPU or memory.
**curl command (conceptual):**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/vulnerable-endpoint?payload=<malicious_input>"
```
The server becomes unresponsive or crashes, confirming the denial of service.

Finding_Name: RCE via LangBot MCP Configuration
Description: The LangBot application allows authenticated remote code execution through the manipulation of MCP (Model Context Protocol) configuration settings. The issue stems from unsanitized input being processed by the system's command execution handler. An attacker can inject arbitrary system commands into the configuration, leading to full server-side compromise.
PoC:
An authenticated user with configuration privileges accesses the MCP settings panel in LangBot. The attacker inputs malicious shell commands into the configuration fields provided for custom server hooks. Upon saving the configuration, the server executes these commands with the privileges of the application process. This allows the attacker to take complete control of the hosting server environment.

**Technical Details:**
```
POST /vulnerable-endpoint HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

param=value; id
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl -X POST "https://target.com/vulnerable-endpoint" -d "param=value; id"
```
The server executes the injected command and returns the output, confirming RCE.

Finding_Name: Insecure Token Store Permissions in garminconnect
Description: The garminconnect application assigns insecure file or storage permissions to its Garmin OAuth token store. The vulnerability is caused by an improper access control implementation that allows local users to read tokens meant to be protected. An attacker can gain unauthorized access to these tokens to impersonate the user's Garmin account across linked services.
PoC: A local attacker with low-privilege access navigates to the directory storing OAuth tokens for the garminconnect application. The attacker observes that the file permissions allow universal read and write access. The attacker copies the stored token files to their own workstation. With these tokens, the attacker can now impersonate the authorized user's sessions to fetch sensitive health and activity data.

Finding_Name: Authenticated SSRF in Koel Radio Stations
Description: The Koel application allows authenticated users to perform a full-read server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack through the Subsonic internet radio station creation feature. The vulnerability is caused by missing host validation for external radio URLs, which allows the server to connect to arbitrary internal endpoints. An attacker can use this to retrieve sensitive data from internal network infrastructure.
PoC:
An authenticated user creates a new radio station entry in Koel using a URL that points to an internal resource. The server attempts to connect to the internal service and fetches data from it. The application then displays or processes the response, which may contain internal configuration data or API credentials. This gives the attacker access to information reachable only from the server's network.

**Technical Details:**
```

Host: target.com
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
```

Finding_Name: Authenticated Blind SSRF in Koel Podcasts
Description: Koel is vulnerable to authenticated blind server-side request forgery via the Subsonic podcast channel creation interface. The application fails to validate the target URL, allowing attackers to trigger outgoing HTTP requests to internal network segments. Because the application does not return the response directly, this represents a blind SSRF vector used for internal reconnaissance.
PoC:
An authenticated user provides a URL targeting an internal port on the host machine during podcast creation. The application attempts to connect to the provided URL for channel metadata. The attacker observes the time taken for the request to return, allowing them to map open and closed ports on the internal network. This reconnaissance facilitates further exploitation of services behind the server's firewall.

**Technical Details:**
```
GET /fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl "https://target.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
```
The server returns internal metadata, confirming SSRF.

Finding_Name: Unauthorized Issue Status Change in MantisBT
Description: The MantisBT REST API allows unauthorized users to modify issue statuses. The vulnerability exists due to a missing authorization check when processing status update requests in the API layer. An attacker can exploit this to change the status of tickets regardless of their assigned permissions or project constraints.
PoC: An authenticated user sends a PATCH request to the MantisBT REST API endpoint to modify an issue status. The attacker targets an issue ID that they are not normally permitted to manage. The server updates the status without verifying if the user has the required project-level privileges. This results in the compromise of the bug tracking workflow integrity.

Finding_Name: RCE via Class Hoisting in MantisBT
Description: MantisBT is vulnerable to remote code execution due to improper eval() usage in class hoisting within the adm_config_set.php file. The application insecurely handles configuration inputs, allowing for the injection of arbitrary PHP code into the class loading logic. An attacker with administrative privileges can gain control of the underlying operating system.
PoC:
An administrator submits a modified configuration payload through the adm_config_set.php interface. The application processes this payload by passing it into an eval() function that handles dynamic class hoisting. The injected PHP code is executed within the context of the web server process. This results in full system compromise for the attacker.

**Technical Details:**
```
POST /vulnerable-endpoint HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

param=value; id
```

**curl command:**
```bash
curl -X POST "https://target.com/vulnerable-endpoint" -d "param=value; id"
```
The server executes the injected command and returns the output, confirming RCE.

Finding_Name: SOAP API Auth Bypass in MantisBT
Description: The MantisBT SOAP API contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that permits privilege escalation to the administrator role. The root cause is a flaw in how the API verifies session tokens during request processing. An attacker can exploit this to bypass standard login requirements and perform administrative actions on the application.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker sends a specially crafted request to the MantisBT SOAP API endpoint. The request uses an altered authentication header that the system mistakenly accepts as valid. The system authenticates the user as an administrator session without verifying credentials. This allows the attacker to execute any API function, including user management and system setting modifications.
